slides.title: Local AI Developer Stack, On-Device
slides.subtitle: Surface Laptop Ultra with NVIDIA RTX Spark
slides.notes: Today we walk through a local AI developer stack running on one Surface Laptop Ultra: code generation, retrieval over internal docs, and hybrid routing to cloud. Every number comes from measurements on this device. Our ask at the end is a 10-developer, 2-week technical pilot.

slides.title: Hardware and runtimes, top to bottom
slides.takeaway: One laptop hosts the full local AI developer stack.

layers.label: Developer tools

layers.label: NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X
layers.detail: Blackwell RTX GPU and 20 CPU cores

slides.notes: Top of the stack is what developers touch: code generation and retrieval over internal docs. Underneath sit two runtimes, llama.cpp build 11573 native ARM64 with CUDA and Foundry Local with the CUDA execution provider. They draw on 28 installed open models, 315 GiB on disk, running on the RTX Spark N1X with 20 CPU cores.

slides.title: Three distinct views of memory
slides.takeaway: Each number is a different view; never add them together.
slides.notes: Architects always ask about memory, so here are the honest numbers. 128 GB is installed. Windows reports about 64 GB visible. nvidia-smi reports a 64,000 MiB GPU memory budget. These are distinct views of memory, not separate pools to sum. We plan model fit against the GPU budget.

slides.title: Two runtimes, one local catalog
slides.takeaway: llama.cpp and Foundry Local serve 28 open models with CUDA.
slides.notes: Two runtimes share one local catalog. llama.cpp runs as a native ARM64 build with CUDA; Foundry Local uses the CUDA execution provider. Twenty-eight open models are installed, 315 GiB on disk, so teams can choose the right model per task instead of standardizing on one.

slides.title: Single-stream decode speed, measured here
slides.takeaway: MoE models decode far faster than a dense 27B model.

data.caption: Local-AI-Bench, Oct 2026, shared machine; not a guaranteed spec

slides.notes: Single-stream decode on this device: Qwen3-Coder 30B about 86 tokens per second with 0.13 seconds to first token, Gemma 4 26B about 72, dense Qwen3.6 27B about 13. Measured with Local-AI-Bench in October 2026 on a shared machine, so treat these as observations, not guaranteed specs or device comparisons.

slides.title: Throughput across concurrent streams
slides.takeaway: One device can serve several developer streams at once.
slides.notes: Concurrency matters for team use. Qwen3-Coder 30B reached about 140 tokens per second aggregate across 4 streams; Gemma 4 26B about 245 across 8 streams. Time to first token for Qwen3-Coder was 0.13 seconds. Shared-machine measurements; the pilot will validate real developer workloads.

slides.title: MoE vs dense: specialists on call
slides.takeaway: MoE activates only a few experts per token, so it decodes faster.
slides.notes: Think of a machine shop. A dense model makes every worker touch every part. A mixture-of-experts model has a big roster, but the foreman calls in only the specialists each job needs. Qwen3-Coder 30B activates about 3B parameters per token, which is why it decodes several times faster than dense Qwen3.6 27B. Speed, not accuracy.

slides.title: Model sizing bands for planning
slides.takeaway: Bands guide capacity planning; larger is not more accurate.
slides.notes: We plan in four bands: S is 1 to 4B parameters, M 7 to 8B, L 14 to 20B, XL 24 to 32B. Bands are planning estimates for memory and speed, not accuracy tiers. A larger parameter count does not mean better answers; the pilot measures acceptance rate to judge quality.

slides.title: Codegen and RAG on the local lane
slides.takeaway: Code and internal docs stay local; heaviest reasoning can route to cloud.

elements.label: Local lane: this Surface Laptop Ultra

slides.notes: Here is the architecture. Requests from the IDE hit a hybrid router. Sensitive, frequent work, code and internal engineering docs, stays on the local lane: llama.cpp or Foundry Local serving Qwen3-Coder 30B, with a local retrieval index supplying context. Only the heaviest reasoning routes to cloud models. This is a routing policy, not an air-gapped claim.

slides.title: Hybrid routing: make or buy
slides.takeaway: Keep sensitive, frequent work local; send the heaviest jobs to cloud.
slides.notes: Zava already makes this decision on the factory floor. Proprietary parts are machined in-house; oversized runs go to a contract factory. Hybrid routing applies the same make-or-buy logic: CAD, PLM and source-code tasks stay on the local lane, while the heaviest reasoning can go to cloud models. Engineering sets the policy.
